title: Checkpoint: Modern and Global
objective: After this level you can weigh what modern writers around the world changed about how stories are told, and why.
summary: From Gitanjali (1912) to Macondo (1967), writers broke forms after World War I and took over their own stories beyond Europe: fragments, flowing minds, new voices, deadpan miracles.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: modern writers broke the old rules. Which ones, and why?
cards.body: Between a Bengali songbook in 1912 and a Colombian town in 1967, writers changed how stories get told. Here is the chapter in order, what changed, and two answers to why.

events.label: Tagore's Gitanjali appears in his own English
Joyce's Ulysses and Eliot's The Waste Land
The Great Gatsby and Mrs. Dalloway
García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude

items.label: The shape
points: Poems built from fragments (The Waste Land)
Thought on the page as it flows

items.label: The teller
points: Achebe tells an Igbo story from the inside
Tagore in his own English words

items.label: The real
points: A salesman wakes as a monstrous vermin
Miracles told with a grandmother's straight face

cards.headline: Two answers to why
cards.body: Look back at the causes this chapter gave. One came from inside Europe: World War I shook faith in Western society and culture, and writers answered with disillusion and broken forms, from Owen's "old Lie" to Eliot's fragments. The other came from beyond Europe: writers like Achebe set out to correct the stories others had told about their people's past. New shapes, new tellers.

questions.prompt: Put these modern and global works in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: Gitanjali came in 1912, Die Verwandlung in 1915, Ulysses in 1922, The Great Gatsby in 1925, Things Fall Apart in 1958 and One Hundred Years of Solitude in 1967.

questions.prompt: Owen's "old Lie" and Eliot's fragments share one cause, by the usual account of modernism. What is it?

options.label: A new fashion for Latin American novels
World War I shaking faith in Western society and culture
The first Nobel Prize for a writer outside Europe
options.rationale: That was Tagore's, in 1913, for other reasons.

options.label: A rediscovery of clay tablets at Nineveh
options.rationale: Nineveh's tablets were dug up in the 1800s, long before these poems.

questions.explanation: The enormity of World War I undermined faith in the foundations of Western society and culture, and postwar writing answered with disillusionment and fragmentation.

questions.prompt: A novel follows two strangers' thoughts through one day in a city, while a clock strikes the hours. Which modernist book is it most like?

options.label: Things Fall Apart
options.rationale: That follows an Igbo village over years, not minds on one day.

options.label: The Great Gatsby
options.rationale: Nick narrates one summer from outside Gatsby's head.

questions.explanation: Mrs. Dalloway moves between Clarissa's and Septimus's minds through one London day, with Big Ben marking the hours.

questions.prompt: Eliot's notes and Kafka's schoolwork both lead back to one ancient poem. Which one?

options.label: The Epic of Gilgamesh
options.rationale: Neither Eliot's notes nor Kafka's schoolwork point there.

options.label: Japan's Kojiki
options.rationale: That's a record of Japanese myths, not their source.

options.label: Babylon's Enuma Elish
options.rationale: That's a Babylonian creation story, recited at the New Year festival.

questions.explanation: Eliot's notes quote Ovid on Tiresias and cite him for Philomela, and Kafka translated part of the Metamorphoses at school, a poem where every story has a transformation.

questions.prompt: Who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 for verse "in his own English words"?

options.label: Wilfred Owen
options.rationale: Owen was killed in 1918 with few poems in print.

questions.explanation: Tagore, the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, was cited for his poetic thought expressed in his own English words.
